summary: This RFC discusses experiments in synchronizing clocks in the ARPA Internet. It argues that a good time-of-day service is neglected in network design, and that accurate clocks help trace complex activity. It asks for discussion.

eli5.summary: People tried getting computers far apart to agree on the exact time, and wrote down what they learned.

questions: why are accurate network clocks useful
how can computers keep synchronized clocks
how accurate can network time be
what is a reference clock in networking
subtitle: Experiments in synchronizing clocks across computer networks.

tldr.problem: Computer networks lacked accurate, synchronized clocks across geographically distributed hosts, making it hard to trace complex transactions or coordinate time-sensitive operations. Each host had its own oscillator, and they drifted apart.
tldr.mechanism: Mills designed a distributed algorithm where hosts periodically exchange timing messages, measure network delays, and continuously adjust their local clocks using a smoothing mechanism that prevents the clock from running backwards. Reference clocks locked to NBS radio broadcasts (WWVB, GOES, WWV) provide the absolute time standard.
tldr.outcome: Experiments across the ARPA Internet and DCnet showed clocks could be synchronized to within tens of milliseconds using ordinary network links. Power-grid clocks offered modest accuracy. The protocol became part of the Distributed Computer Network (DCnet) architecture.

today: RFC 957 documents foundational work in network time synchronization that led to the development of the Network Time Protocol (NTP), now a critical infrastructure component of the Internet. The algorithms and principles Mills developed remain relevant in NTP version 4 and later. The work showed that accurate, distributed timekeeping across networks is both necessary and achievable, enabling applications that depend on precise timestamps and coordinating events across systems separated by continents.

sections.title: Why Network Clocks Matter
sections.content:
One important service frequently neglected in network design is a high-quality, accurate time-of-day clock. Such a service would be useful for tracing complex transactions (knowing which event happened first), synchronizing cached databases (keeping distributed copies consistent), monitoring network performance, and isolating problems (correlating events across the network).

The Internet protocol suite already included mechanisms to record and transmit time, such as the ICMP Timestamp message and the Time Protocol. However, the challenge was maintaining synchronized clocks across many hosts when each host has its own oscillator that drifts at different rates, and network delays make it hard to measure exact times.

RFC 957 describes experiments in synchronizing clocks across the ARPA Internet using a distributed algorithm developed for the Distributed Computer Network (DCnet). The approach has been in use since 1979 and was continuously tested and refined.
sections.eli5: Without synchronized clocks, it is hard to know which event happened first when computers are far apart. This RFC describes a way to keep their clocks in sync.

sections.title: The Logical Clock
sections.content:
Each host maintains a logical clock using software and hardware. The core is a 48-bit Clock Register that increments at 1000 Hz, providing precise sub-second timestamps. A 32-bit Clock-Adjust Register controls how fast the clock slews (runs at a different rate) in response to corrections from the network. A Counter Register in the clock interface provides the fine-grained timing.

When a correction arrives from the network (as a signed 32-bit integer in milliseconds), the mechanism applies it differently depending on the magnitude. For small corrections (less than 128 ms), the clock gradually slews toward the correct time using a smoothing mechanism. This ensures the clock never runs backwards, which could confuse applications. For large corrections (greater than 128 ms), the mechanism waits for a consistent signal before making a jump, protecting against transient errors.

The slewing rate is proportional to the correction magnitude: large errors are fixed quickly, but small corrections are applied slowly, providing high stability. The algorithm uses a divisor of 256 to spread corrections over time, achieving a maximum slew-rate of about 125 microseconds per second with a granularity of about 2 microseconds.
sections.eli5: The clock has gears that adjust its speed to match the real time. When it is wrong by a little, it slowly spins the gears to catch up. When it is very wrong, it waits to see if that is really true, then makes a big jump.

sections.title: Distributing Timing Across the Network
sections.content:
The algorithm is distributed: each host maintains synchronization information about every other host. Hosts communicate via periodic Hello messages that carry timing data and are exchanged about every 30 seconds or less. These same Hello messages are also used by the routing algorithm.

Each Hello message includes a timestamp inserted at transmission time and information to accurately compute roundtrip delays between hosts. When a host receives a Hello message, it extracts the timestamp and compares it to its local clock, computing a correction sample. It also looks at the precomputed delay and offset information for distant hosts included in the message.

A Host Table at each host stores the computed roundtrip delay and clock offset to every other host. The routing algorithm uses this table to select which neighbor to forward timing corrections through. A host only accepts corrections from neighbors on the minimum-delay path to the reference clock. If there is no route to the reference clock, the local clock free-runs at its own intrinsic rate (usually a crystal oscillator).
sections.eli5: Hosts send each other friendly messages every 30 seconds saying 'here is what I think the time is.' Each host listens to the neighbors closest to a clock that knows the real time, and adjusts based on what those neighbors say.

sections.title: Reference Clocks and Accuracy
sections.content:
The accuracy of the entire network depends on the reference clock used as the standard. RFC 957 describes experiments using three commercial precision reference clocks synchronized to NBS broadcasts:

WWVB (60 kHz radio broadcast): Claims one-millisecond accuracy. About 2 milliseconds absolute accuracy after accounting for propagation delays and interrupt latencies.

GOES satellite (UHF broadcast): Also claims one-millisecond accuracy. Provides similar results to WWVB.

WWV (HF radio, 5, 10, 15 MHz): Claims 100-millisecond accuracy but was measured somewhat better in practice.

Each reference clock is connected to a reference host via a serial line. About once every 30 seconds, the host driver compares the reference clock's absolute time with the host's logical clock and generates a correction. This reference host then corrects all other hosts in the network. The experiments measured offsets as clocks synchronized, showing they settled within tens of milliseconds of the reference.
sections.eli5: A special clock connected to a radio broadcast knows the real time. Every 30 seconds it tells the network hosts 'here is what the real time is,' and the hosts adjust based on that.

sections.title: Experimental Results
sections.content:
Experiments conducted in late June and July 1985 involved six hosts and three reference clocks across DCnet and connected to the ARPANET. The tests collected measurements over an 11-day period, coinciding with the insertion of a leap second, which tested system stability during disruptions.

For power-grid clocks, experiments showed that electric utilities slew their grid frequency to balance load. The eastern grid showed gains of 4 to 6 seconds during evening hours and losses during the day, with maximum slewing rates about 400 ppm. A host locked to the power grid (DCN7) remained typically within 30 ms of the reference host and infrequently exceeded 100 ms. Over seven days, the mean offset was less than one millisecond with standard deviation about 24 ms.

For network-synchronized clocks, hosts across different link types (Ethernet, point-to-point DDCMP, asynchronous serial) all maintained good synchronization. The algorithm successfully filtered transient errors caused by link retransmissions and host reboots.

For radio clock accuracy, WWVB and GOES clocks proved reliable and accurate. The experiments confirmed that distributed clock synchronization was practical and achieved the required accuracy for tracing transactions and correlating events across the network.
sections.eli5: When they tested it, clocks stayed within tens of milliseconds of each other. Clocks on the power grid were less stable but still worked. The system easily handled the leap second event that is thrown in every few years.
